text: The rash flares up every summer.
It is spreading this week, faster than before.
Good morning, Mrs. Parker. I am Doctor Wached. What brings you in today?
I have this rash on my hands. It started about three weeks ago, on the back of the right hand, and now it is on both.
So it started on one hand and it is spreading. Does it itch?
It is very itchy at night. During the day I hardly notice it, and then I wake up at two in the morning scratching.
Is it itching right now, while we are talking?
No, not at this moment. It is tender if I press it, though. I tried an over-the-counter cream for ten days and it did nothing.
Thank you. Does anything like this run in the family?
My mother had eczema all her life. Hers used to flare up in winter and then settle down again. Is that what I have?
Good morning. I am Doctor Wached. What brings you in today?
Are you taking anything for it at the moment?
Let me examine your hands, and then I will explain what we do next.

The first thing I learned in residency was that the patient tells you the diagnosis in the first ninety seconds, if you let them. The temptation is to interrupt. You hear the word rash, you already have three questions ready, and you jump in. And the moment you do that, something changes in the room: the patient stops telling you the story and starts answering your questions instead. The real complaint, the thing that actually made them pick up the phone, stays unsaid. So I hold my questions. I ask two things and then I close my mouth: what brings you in today, and what worries you most about it. The second one is the one people forget, and it is the one that tells you why they came now and not six months ago. Only after that do I look at the skin. And one more thing about the word itchy. Patients use it for very different things. Some mean a small irritation, some mean they are awake at three in the morning tearing at their arms. So I always ask two questions, not one: does it itch at night, and is it itching right now, while we are sitting here. The two answers are almost never the same, and the difference between them tells you more than the photograph does.

I put off calling the clinic for a month, because I kept telling myself it was nothing. That is the honest answer. The rash came and went. It would get red and angry for four or five days, and then it would settle down, and every time it settled down I thought, well, there we are, it is going away, no need to bother anybody. Then it would come back. What finally changed things was my daughter. She stayed over one weekend, and she saw me scratching in my sleep. She did not say much about it. She just picked up my phone the next morning and booked the appointment herself, and then she told me she had done it. I was annoyed for about an hour and then I was grateful. And I will tell you what I was most afraid of hearing, because I think about it every time I sit in a waiting room. I was not afraid that it would be serious. I was afraid that it would be serious and that somebody would tell me I had waited too long to come in.

Good morning. I am Doctor Wached. What brings you in today? So the rash started on one hand and it is spreading. Does it itch at night? Are you taking anything for it at the moment? Does anything like this run in the family? Let me examine your hands, and then I will explain what we do next.
The rash is spreading faster this week.
She uses the cream every morning.
